title: Chapter 2: Retained
blurb: The dog on floor 5 has rules for Ravi, and one he won't explain.

blocks.text: "Hold the doors, son," the dog said. "Downstairs I'm a dog, and dogs don't explain."
I put my thumb on the brass button marked OPEN. I didn't decide to. Four months of nights does that to you: somebody says hold the lift, you hold the lift.

I'd talked to Dusty every night since I started. About the boiler, about the bins, about the lift's habit of stopping an inch proud of the ground floor so the tenants catch their toes on it. He'd never once answered, which was most of what I liked about him. Now he had, and for the first time in four months I couldn't think of a single thing to say to him.
"Your book's filled up since you left it," he said. "Seven orders on this floor. You've closed one. Every one you sign, you carry. That's what I wanted you told before you signed another."
The bulbs hummed all the way down a corridor that wasn't on any drawing. The dog looked at my thumb, to check it was still on the button.
"You're Dusty," I said, which wasn't much of a contribution.
"Tenants call me that. Name's Walter Ossery. I had your job before you. I wrote your advert."

W. Ossery. The name at the bottom of the advert I'd answered. The man from the Trust who gave me the keys had said the old super had retired, and I'd pictured a bungalow somewhere with a greenhouse. I had not pictured the mat under the post table.
"Then why," I said, and stopped, because there isn't a polite way to ask a man why he's a lurcher. "Why are you a dog, Mr Ossery?"
"Walter. I was retained." He stood and shook himself, ears flapping, and looked off down the corridor. "Now. You signed that slip and the cough came. Yes?"

Retained. I turned it over the way you turn over a noise in a wall. A retaining wall holds back what would otherwise fall on you. A retainer is what you pay a man to stay. Neither of them turns a man into a dog. So the building had done it. He'd had this job a long time, by the look of his notes, and somewhere in it he'd done something the building didn't like, cut a corner or skimped a joint, and this was what it did to you for that. I decided that, standing there with my thumb on the button, and it frightened me more than the corridor had.

"Yes," I said. "It came when I signed it and it went when I signed it off. I worked that out. I'm not sure I worked it out right. Is it every order? Is it always a cough? Is it the same cough for every job?"
"Every order. Its own trouble. A leak's a wet chest. A draught'll be something else. It's on the slip."
"Right."
"You carry it wherever you go. Your bed. The bus. Your mother's for Sunday dinner. Till you sign it off at the fault, or—" He stopped. "Till you sign it off."
"Or what?"
"And seven days," he said, as if I hadn't spoken. "Hold one open seven days, it gets worse. Another seven, worse again. Sign it, the clock starts. So you sign what you mean to finish."
"And if I don't sign them at all?"

"They sit. They get worse slower. They still get worse." He looked down at the floor of the cage, and I'd swear he looked through it, at four floors of people asleep. "Leave them long enough and they come through. Like your one tonight."
I thought of 4D's kitchen wall running in the torchlight, and Lou Mabbott with every towel she owned on the lino.
"You're grade nought," Walter said. "Look at your header. Nought carries one. One at a time, son, and you'll be all right."
"What happens if I sign for two?"

"You don't. The book won't take your name." He sat again. "Go and look at a job first. Then sign it in the book, write what's wrong in the cause line, bring the slip up, mend it where it is, and sign it off there. Not in the office. There."
"I know that bit."
"You know it once. Know it seven times."
I took my thumb off the button to rub my face, and the doors began to fold, and I put it back. "Is there anything else? Before I go down and pretend I didn't have this conversation with the dog?"
"One thing." He looked up at me from under his eyebrows. "Never take a raise from anyone but me."
I waited for the rest of it. There wasn't any.
"You're a dog," I said.
"I am."
"So you can't give me a raise."
"Then you won't be getting one, will you." He lay down across my boots. "Press G, son. It's gone four."

In the lobby he got up off my boots, walked to his mat under the post table, turned round three times and lay down with a sigh, and when I said, "Walter?" he flicked one ear and went to sleep. I stood there at four in the morning, talking to a lurcher about whether he wanted the end of the milk, and he sighed at exactly the right moment, the way he always had.
The Works Book was open on the desk in the office. I hadn't left it open. I'd stopped expecting to.
``` PELLORY COURT. FLOOR 5. TIER 1.

WO-5-001  LEAK, COLD RISER           CLOSED WO-5-002  RISER 2, JOINTS FAILING    OPEN WO-5-003  DOOR 5-1, SWOLLEN IN FRAME OPEN WO-5-004  STAIRWELL, DRAUGHT         OPEN WO-5-005  SLAB, RISING DAMP          OPEN WO-5-006  CORRIDOR LIGHTS, FLICKER   OPEN WO-5-007  DADO, GRIME (CRAWLING)     OPEN ```

Six lines in red and one in black, and the black one was mine. I read it twice, lips moving, the way I read anything that wants my name on it. A stairwell on a floor with no stairs to it. A slab under a floor the street couldn't see. Grime, with a word in brackets after it that I could have done without.
"Right," I told the book. "Not tonight."
Then I looked up, and the advert was looking back at me.

It had been on the wall since before I came: a cutting from the small ads in a cheap black frame, pinned between the index cards as if the old super couldn't bear to throw it out. I'd seen it every night for four months. I hadn't read it since the day I answered it.
``` NIGHT SUPERINTENDENT. 380 A WEEK CASH. NO LICENCE REQUIRED. APPLY IN WRITING. W. OSSERY, 14 WICKLINE ST. ```

I read it twice. Never take a raise from anyone but me. The Trust were tight; that was all he'd meant. Every old hand I'd worked under had said a version of it about every landlord they'd had: don't wait on them for money, and if they ever offer, check what they want back. Walter had just said it the way you'd say it to a lad on his first site, with a joke on the end, and the joke was that he was a dog.

The building's drawings lived in a cardboard tube behind the door, linen-backed, dated 1925. I unrolled them on the desk and held the corners down with the kettle and the Works Book and looked for a fifth floor for a long time. Four storeys and a roof, the way the street saw it. Not even a gap where one might go. I rolled them up and put them back, and I didn't tell myself there'd be a sensible reason, because I'd said that to the dog last night and the dog had answered.

At eight I put 4D's kitchen lights back on, as I'd promised. Lou opened the door in a dressing gown with a mug in each hand and gave me one before I could say no. Danny was at the table eating cereal with his coat already on.
"Why was the light off?" he asked.
"Fuse," said Lou, and looked at me over his head. "Roof all right?"

"It'll hold," I said, which was true of a coupling on a riser on a floor that didn't exist, and near enough to the roof for Lou. I drank the tea without looking at her ceiling. I thanked her for it, and for the banana bread, and for not ringing the Trust, and she told me to go to bed before I thanked the kettle.
I slept till three, and at eleven that night I rode up with Walter to look first.

The draught was at the far end of the corridor, past both riser cupboards, behind a door with wired glass in it and a brass plate that said STAIRS. Beyond the glass a stair went up into smooth plaster and down into solid brick, and through the gap under the door came a long, low howl, like wind across the neck of a bottle, from a stairwell that had nowhere for wind to come from.

The grime was on the dado rail halfway along: a brown film about a hand wide, and when I watched it for a while it moved. Slowly, the way a shadow moves on a sunny afternoon, uphill towards the nearest bulb.

Riser 2 was behind a door with its own brass plate, three doors on from the one I'd fixed. The cast-iron joints were weeping all the way down the run, every one a dark sweating collar, and inside the pipe chase something small went pattering downward, towards the flats, and stopped when I held my breath.
"Draught first," Walter said. "It's quickest."

In the office I signed WO-5-004 to take it and wrote the cause in my fence-post hand: STAIR DOOR CLOSER SPRING BROKEN, SEAL PERISHED. I'd seen the closer arm hanging loose. The slip said SYMPTOM: COLD EXTREMITIES. EARACHE. My fingers went cold as the pen lifted, a deep blue cold like holding a bag of frozen peas too long, and my ears started to ache from the inside, the way they do on a bus stop in January.
I took a new closer and a brush strip out of the SPARES box with hands I could hardly feel, and rode up.

Close to, the howl got into my teeth. It wasn't loud. It was patient. It was the sound a building makes in a film just before somebody goes down to the cellar, and I was the somebody, and I didn't like that at all, so I talked to it.
"Right," I told the draught. "I'm sorry about the cold hands. Ten minutes and you're shut."
"Don't chat to it, son," Walter said, from behind me. "Mend it."
"I'm doing both."

I got the old closer off, which took longer than it should because my fingers were made of wood. I told the door it had been very brave. I fitted the new arm and set the spring and told the draught what I was doing at every turn of the screwdriver, because if I stopped talking I'd have to listen to it. The howl thinned as the door swung true. I cut the brush strip to length, screwed it along the bottom rail, let the door close on its own and heard the latch catch.
The howl stopped. Just stopped, like someone had put a hand over its mouth. I looked at my watch. Nine minutes.
I signed the slip on my knee at the door. The ink went black, my hands came back to me in a rush of pins and needles, and my ears stopped hurting.
"Told you," I said to the door. "Ten minutes."
"Nine," said Walter.

The grime took longer. My first theory, as I'd stood watching it, was mould: brown, damp-loving, on the cold side of a corridor in a building that leaked. Mould would have meant fixing the damp first, and the damp was the slab, and the slab was a different order. But when I got up close with a torch it was greasy, not furry, and it wasn't spreading out from a patch the way mould does. It was coming from somewhere, in a line, out of a little cast grille above the dado that had been an extract vent, once, for a kitchen floor 5 didn't have. The grille was clogged solid. The grease was backing up out of it and going looking for the light.

So I went down, signed WO-5-007, wrote EXTRACT GRILLE BLOCKED, GREASE BACKING UP, and an itch started on the backs of my wrists and walked slowly up my forearms under my sleeves, uphill, towards my elbows. I scrubbed the dado with sugar soap and fitted a new grille from the box and scratched my arms raw in between. When I signed the slip under the bulb, the itch went, and the brown film on the wall went dull and stayed where it was, and a cloth took it off in one wipe.
Back in the office, at twenty to two, the header had moved.
``` CARETAKER: R. ANAND GRADE: 0 CREDITS: 3 HOLDING: 0 CERTIFIED: NONE ```
I'd have liked it to say something kinder. It didn't do kind. It did numbers, and the numbers were going the right way.

I could have stopped. Walter had gone back up to his mat in the lobby and back to being a dog who couldn't advise me, which was convenient for him. I had seven days on anything I signed, and the riser wanted parts I didn't have: a run of joints, not one, and the merchant on Ropewalk Lane didn't open till half seven. I could have waited till I had the parts in my hand and signed it then, and saved myself five hours of carrying it.
But I'd heard the thing in the pipe chase going down. Riser 2 ran past the flats, all four floors of them, and the order on the page said so in its own words.

``` WO-5-002 FLOOR 5. TIER 1. FAULT: RISER 2, JOINTS FAILING. LEAK. PEST PASSAGE TO FLOORS 1-4. CAUSE: UNDIAGNOSED. GRADE REQUIRED: 1. SYMPTOM: WET CHILL. WATERY COUGH. STATUS: OPEN. TAKEN BY: ______________ ```
I knew exactly what it would cost. That was the difference between this and last night. I read it twice, and at two o'clock by the office clock I signed it.
The chill came in under my breastbone like fog off the estuary, and I coughed, and the cough had water in it.
"Hello again," I said to it.

I went up the public stairs to see the bottom end of the job, because I couldn't sit in the office with it. Riser 2's cupboard on the fourth-floor landing was dry, but there was a tidemark on its back wall I didn't remember, and a scatter of droppings no bigger than rice on the floor of it, and when I put my ear to the casing I heard the patter again, a long way up, coming down.
I coughed. I tried to do it quietly, into my elbow, and it came out like a drain clearing.
Across the landing, the door of 4C opened on its chain.
"Mr Caretaker," said Mrs Wrobel.
"Sorry. Did I wake you? I'm just looking at the riser. There's a tidemark here, and I think there's something living in the—"

The door shut. The chain came off. The door opened again, all the way this time, and Mrs Wrobel stood in it in a quilted dressing gown buttoned to the neck, seventy-one years old and wide awake at half past two in the morning.
"Sit," she said. "Top step. Now."
"I'm fine, honestly. It's a bit of a chest."
"Sit."

I sat on the top step. She went inside, and through the open door I could see a coat on the hook that wasn't hers, a man's coat, brown, the elbows gone shiny, and a pair of men's slippers set side by side underneath it, as if someone had just stepped out of them. A pan clinked. She came back with a bowl of barley soup so thick the spoon stood up in it, and a slice of rye bread laid across the top like a lid.
"Eat."
"You don't have to—"
"Eat. Then argue."
So I ate, because I always eat what I'm given, and by halfway down the bowl there was no argument left in me. She stood in her doorway with her arms folded and watched me like a sergeant.
"Thank you," I said. "Really. Thank you."
"You said that." She waited till I coughed again. "My husband had a cough like this. Jurek. Years he had it."
"Is he—"

"Dead. Long enough I say it plain." She looked down at the landing between us. "I have it also. Building cough." And, as if to show me, she coughed once, dry, behind her hand, the way she had last night behind her door.

Building cough. I knew that one. A top-floor flat in an old block, a cold roof, soup on the gas every day and the windows shut against the draughts. The steam has to go somewhere, so it goes into the walls, and in the end into the people. Her roof was dry; I'd been up there last night. So it wasn't getting in. It was being made inside and not getting out.
"It might be damp," I said, between spoonfuls. "From the cooking. Does the fan over your cooker still work? If it doesn't, the steam's got nowhere to go but the walls. I could look at it Thursday."
Mrs Wrobel considered me for a long moment, the way you'd consider a wall before you lean on it.
"Thursday," she said. "Bring your own tea."
"I will. Thank you."

"Three times now." She took the empty bowl out of my hands before I could thank her for that too, and filled it again from the pan she'd brought out to the doorway, and gave it back. I coughed. She watched the soup instead of me.
"Which floor were you on, Mr Caretaker?"
"This one," I said. "I was only looking in the riser cupboard. There's a tidemark on the back wall, and I think—"
"No." She said it the way you'd stop a man stepping off a kerb. "Before. Which floor."

Behind me, in the casing, the patter came down again. Not a long way up this time. It came down the last of the run in a rush and stopped a foot above my head, level with the top of the cupboard door, where the fourth floor's ceiling was and the fifth floor wasn't supposed to be. Then something on the other side of the board scratched at a joint. Twice. The way you'd try a door you'd been told was locked.

I coughed, and the cough had water in it, and I started telling her about cast-iron collars and how they weep, because it was that or listen to the scratching. She wasn't listening. She was looking past me at the cupboard, then at her own doorframe, then back, and I watched her measure the distance between the two the way I'd measure a run of pipe.
"Shut that cupboard, Mr Caretaker," she said. "Then tell me which floor."
